name: Ab Wheel Rollout
collapse_rationale: Base core exercise; no more-basic parent lift exists in this vocabulary.

axes.note: Most lifters cannot control the fully extended (prone) position early on and stop the rollout short; full extension is a distinct, much harder progression.
Standing ab wheel rollout is a far more advanced progression of the same movement pattern.

unmapped_notes: This is a bodyweight-ROM movement with no external load metric in normal use, so no strength_coefficient/percentile concern applies to either axis; difficulty scales with ROM/lever length, not load moved.

name: Barbell Row
collapse_rationale: Base bent-over rowing pattern; Pendlay/Yates rows are grip-orientation qualifiers of this same lift, not distinct patterns.

axes.note: Pronated (overhand) is the standard bent-over row; supinated (Yates row) shifts emphasis toward lats/biceps and is commonly reported as allowing similar or slightly heavier loads by lifters, though this is coaching consensus rather than controlled study.
Wider grip shortens the pull ROM and biases upper-back/rear-delt involvement.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Coaching consensus (Yates-style supinated rows) suggests comparable or slightly higher loads, but no controlled 1RM comparison study was found; too weak to assign a numeric ratio.

unmapped_notes: Chest-supported row is a distinct machine/bench setup, not modeled as a qualifier of this free-standing lift.

name: Burpee
collapse_rationale: Standalone bodyweight conditioning complex; no meaningful equipment/positional qualifiers in common practice.
unmapped_notes: Variations (push-up burpee, tuck-jump burpee, burpee box jump) are effectively distinct exercises/combos rather than qualifier values on a single closed vocabulary axis.

name: Cable Reverse Curl
collapse_rationale: Same cable low-pulley curl pattern; the only change is a pronated (overhand) grip instead of the default supinated grip, shifting emphasis to the brachialis/forearm extensors.

axes.note: EZ-bar softens wrist strain in the pronated position; both are commonly used.
Minor stance/hand-width variation; no strong consensus on effect.

strength_coefficients.rationale: EMG literature and coaching sources consistently report reverse (pronated) curls allow noticeably lighter loads than supinated curls because biceps brachii contributes less and brachialis/forearm extensors carry more of the work, but no source gave a defensible numeric ratio.

name: Conventional Deadlift
collapse_rationale: Base hip-hinge pulling pattern; sumo and trap-bar deadlift are treated as distinct motor patterns/lifts, not qualifiers of this one.

axes.note: Grip orientation is a grip-security choice, not a mechanical-leverage change to the pull itself.
Bands/chains alter the resistance curve through the pull, common in powerlifting accessory work.

axes.custom_hint: e.g. 2-inch deficit, mid-shin block
axes.note: Deficit increases ROM (harder); block/rack pulls shorten ROM (typically allows more load); paused adds a dead-stop.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Grip orientation only changes how the bar is secured, not the lift's biomechanics, once grip strength is sufficient; it does not systematically change achievable load for the pull itself.
Deficit deadlifts are widely reported as harder due to increased ROM from a longer starting stretch, but no controlled percentage figure was found.
Rack/block pulls shorten the ROM and typically allow substantially heavier loads than a full pull, but the magnitude depends heavily on block height, so no single defensible ratio exists.

name: Diamond Push-Up
collapse_rationale: Same bodyweight pressing pattern with hands brought together under the chest; the closed vocabulary's closest match is grip_width: close, though the true hand shape (touching thumbs/forefingers forming a diamond) is narrower than a typical 'close grip' bench variant.

axes.note: A weighted vest is the common way to progressively load this bodyweight movement.
Full ROM touches chest to hands; partial reps are a common beginner regression.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Diamond push-ups are consistently described as harder than standard push-ups (reduced leverage, more triceps demand, less pec involvement), but as a bodyweight movement measured in reps rather than load, no defensible load-ratio figure exists; excluding protects users who only do the harder variant.

unmapped_notes: The exact hand shape (fingers/thumbs touching, forming a diamond) is narrower than the closed vocabulary's generic 'close' grip_width value.

name: Dumbbell Skull Crusher
collapse_rationale: Treated as a base lift within this slice; lying triceps extension family, bench-angle and grip choices are qualifiers of it.

axes.note: Incline versions increase shoulder flexion and long-head triceps stretch at the bottom; decline reduces shoulder involvement.
Neutral (hammer-style) grip is common with dumbbells and easier on the wrists/elbows than pronated.
Bringing the dumbbells past the forehead toward the floor (lengthened partial) is a deliberately harder, more stretch-focused variant some lifters use.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Incline skull crushers are commonly described as harder due to greater shoulder flexion and triceps long-head stretch, but no numeric load comparison was found.

name: Glute Kickback Machine
collapse_rationale: Base machine exercise; the machine is inherently single-leg by design, so laterality is not a user choice.
unmapped_notes: No commonly-practiced qualifier choice was identified beyond ROM depth, which most machines don't let the user meaningfully vary; leaving axes empty per brief guidance for exercises without a real choice point.

name: Hanging Leg Raise
collapse_rationale: Base hanging core exercise; bent-knee ('hanging knee raise') is commonly sold as a separate exercise name rather than a qualifier value in this vocabulary, so it is not collapsed here.

axes.note: Full ROM raises straight legs to roughly parallel/above; many lifters only achieve a partial raise.

unmapped_notes: Grip aids (lifting straps, arm slings/ab-straps at a pull-up rig) change how the exercise is held but don't map cleanly onto the attachment axis, which is oriented toward cable/machine attachments.

name: Incline Dumbbell Press
collapse_rationale: Same dumbbell horizontal-pressing pattern as flat dumbbell bench press with the torso inclined; a very common and well-documented qualifier rather than a distinct motor pattern.

axes.note: Higher angles shift emphasis toward the clavicular (upper) pec and anterior deltoid and reduce achievable load.
Neutral grip is often used to reduce shoulder strain at higher incline angles.
Single-arm/alternating incline press adds a rotational core-stability demand.

strength_coefficients.rationale: A study on trained young men found flat barbell bench press 1RM was 28.6% higher than 30-degree incline barbell bench press 1RM (incline/flat ~= 0.78). This is barbell data being applied to a dumbbell exercise, and dumbbell-specific ratios reportedly run even lower (roughly 75-90% of flat dumbbell press per coaching sources), so confidence is downgraded and the value is excluded from percentile rather than normalized.

name: Leg Curl
collapse_rationale: Kept as a base/generic name covering the family of leg curl machines; seated vs. lying prone are genuinely different machines with different resistance curves, modeled here as a body_position qualifier rather than split into separate base exercises, since the founder's tracking use case (hamstring curl PR) is the same across both.

axes.note: Seated and lying-prone leg curl machines have different resistance curves and are commonly discussed as feeling meaningfully different in achievable load.
Many machines support single-leg curls to address side-to-side imbalances.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Seated and lying leg curl machines are frequently reported by lifters/coaches to allow different loads due to differing lever arms and hip-flexion angle, but no controlled comparison study was found to support a numeric ratio.

name: Machine Triceps Extension
collapse_rationale: Base machine exercise; grip is generally fixed by the machine's handles, so grip_orientation is not a real user choice.

axes.note: Some machines have independent single-arm handles.

name: Overhead Squat
collapse_rationale: Distinct motor pattern (overhead-locked bar throughout a full squat) from back/front squat, not a qualifier of either — kept as its own base lift.

axes.note: Wider (snatch-width) grip is standard for weightlifting-style overhead squats; a narrower grip closer to shoulder width is sometimes used for a more stable but shorter-ROM overhead position.
Foot stance mirrors normal squat stance choices.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Weightlifting coaching sources describe a grip closer to shoulder width as a stronger, more sustainable overhead position than a very wide snatch grip, but this is a qualitative stability claim, not a quantified load-capacity ratio.

name: Plate Pinch Hold
collapse_rationale: Base grip-strength static hold exercise.

axes.note: Typically trained and tested one hand at a time, though a two-plate-in-each-hand bilateral variant exists.

unmapped_notes: This is a timed isometric hold rather than a rep-based lift; PR tracking is by weight-held-for-time, and no percentile/strength-coefficient concern applies since there is only one load axis (the plates held), not a technique variant that changes achievable load for a fixed technique.

name: Reverse Hyperextension
collapse_rationale: Base posterior-chain machine/bench exercise.

axes.note: Can be done with just the leg-lever swing or with added plate load on the machine.
Full ROM swings the legs from a dead hang to above hip level.

name: Seated Barbell Press
collapse_rationale: Same vertical barbell pressing pattern as the standing overhead press; seated removes leg drive and lower-body stabilization but is the same lift, not a distinct pattern.

axes.note: Standard vertical-press grip width choices.
A Smith machine version is common where the fixed bar path further removes stabilization demand.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Sources report standing barbell overhead press requires substantially more stabilizer/deltoid activation than seated, and suggest the added stability of a seated position can sometimes allow heavier absolute loads, but no numeric 1RM ratio was found; excluding avoids guessing which direction and magnitude applies to a given lifter.

name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
collapse_rationale: Same hip-hinge RDL pattern performed one leg at a time; the load-bearing leg mechanics and hinge pattern are the same lift with a laterality qualifier, not a distinct movement.

axes.note: Almost always performed with dumbbells or a kettlebell rather than a barbell due to balance demands.
Bodyweight-only version is a common beginner/balance-focused regression.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Research on loading positions in single-leg RDL confirms it is trained with substantially less absolute load than bilateral RDL while increasing demand on hip/trunk stabilizers, but no source gave a defensible percentage figure, and the load reduction is driven heavily by balance/stability rather than pure strength — exactly the case the founder's rule is meant to protect against penalizing.

name: Step-Up
collapse_rationale: Base unilateral-loading leg exercise.

axes.custom_hint: e.g. 12in box, 18in box, exact box height
axes.note: Box/platform height changes knee flexion depth and difficulty substantially.
Alternating switches lead leg each rep; unilateral does all reps on one leg before switching.
Commonly loaded with dumbbells, a barbell, or a weighted vest.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Higher box height increases knee/hip flexion and difficulty, which should reduce achievable load, but no source with a specific figure was found and box height itself varies by user, making a single ratio unreliable.

name: Trap-Bar Deadlift
collapse_rationale: Still a hip-hinge pull to a standing lockout with a loaded bar, tracked by most lifters/apps as a deadlift variant rather than its own family; the founder's Front-Squat/Back-Squat precedent for 'genuinely distinct pattern' arguably applies less here since the pull direction and finish position are the same, even though torso angle is more upright than a conventional pull. Flagged as judgment call, not certainty.

axes.note: Standard plate loading; chains are an occasional accessory variation.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Coaching sources consistently describe trap-bar deadlifts as allowing heavier loads than a conventional straight-bar deadlift due to a more upright torso and (for high-handle versions) reduced range of motion, but a widely-repeated numeric percentage could not be verified against primary source text when fetched directly, so no ratio is reported. Never penalize a trap-bar-only lifter's percentile.

unmapped_notes: High-handle vs. low-handle grip position is a real, commonly-discussed choice that materially changes ROM and load, but this closed vocabulary has no axis for trap-bar handle height specifically; grip_width/stance don't capture it well.

name: Wide-Grip Pull-Up
collapse_rationale: Same vertical pulling pattern as a standard pull-up; only hand spacing and orientation differ.

axes.note: Wider grips reduce elbow-flexion contribution and shorten the effective ROM at the top, generally making the movement harder rep-for-rep.
Pronated (overhand) is the standard pull-up grip; supinated is a chin-up, neutral uses parallel handles.
Progression/regression via added weight or assistance (band/machine).

strength_coefficients.rationale: A controlled study on the related lat pull-down movement found 6RM load with a wide grip (77.3kg) was measurably lower than narrow/medium grip (~80kg), a roughly 4% reduction; however pull-ups are a fixed-bodyweight, moving-body exercise rather than a moving-bar machine pull, so this is only directional evidence, not a load ratio for pull-ups specifically. Excluding protects wide-grip-only pull-up trainees from an unfair percentile penalty.

name: Alternating Dumbbell Curl
collapse_rationale: Same implement and motor pattern as a standard Dumbbell Curl; the only difference is timing/laterality (arms alternate instead of moving together).

axes.note: Alternating vs bilateral is a pacing/coordination choice, not a load change per arm.
Some lifters rotate the wrist through the rep (supinating) or hold neutral (hammer-style) while alternating.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Per-dumbbell load is identical whether both arms move together or alternate; this changes fatigue/pacing, not the weight moved.

No retrieved source quantifies a supinated-vs-neutral dumbbell curl 1RM ratio; neutral grip changes brachialis/brachioradialis contribution and is close enough to a different exercise (hammer curl) to exclude rather than guess.

name: Belt Squat
collapse_rationale: Belt squat uses a fundamentally different loading path (load hangs from a belt at the hips via a dedicated machine or DIY rig) rather than axial spinal loading like a back squat. It is not a qualifier on Back Squat — it is its own base lift.

axes.note: Stance width shifts quad/adductor emphasis similarly to back squat stance changes.
Most belt squat machines/rigs use plates or a weight stack; bands/chains are occasional accommodating-resistance additions.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No belt-squat-specific stance-load research retrieved; belt squat load is already excluded from any back-squat percentile per the exercise-level note below, so stance sub-variants inherit exclude.

unmapped_notes: Sources (Inspire US, Lift Vault, Dr Workout) consistently report belt squat allows less absolute load than back squat because weight hangs from the hips rather than loading the spine, and note high individual variation. Because it is a different lift, not a qualifier, its logged load should never feed a squat percentile at all (handled at the exercise level, not via an axis ratio).

name: Cable Crossover
collapse_rationale: Cable Crossover is commonly treated as its own base name (dual-pulley fly pattern); it is not itself a qualified variant of another logged exercise in this set.

axes.note: High-to-low crossover biases lower pec; low-to-high (floor pulley) biases upper pec.

axes.custom_hint: e.g. loop handle, ball handle
axes.note: Attachment choice is mostly a comfort/grip preference, not a strength difference.
Single-arm crossover is a common unilateral variant used for asymmetry work.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No comparative load research was retrieved for high vs low pulley crossover; per-arm load also isn't a standard percentile lift, so exclude is safe regardless.

name: Cable Rope Hammer Curl
collapse_rationale: Same cable-curl motor pattern as a generic Cable Curl; the rope attachment plus neutral (hammer) grip are the only distinguishing choices.

axes.note: Rope allows the neutral hand path that defines the hammer variant.
Neutral (hammer) grip biases brachialis/brachioradialis over biceps brachii vs a supinated cable curl.
Low pulley origin is standard for a curl pattern.
Rope allows both hands on one rope (bilateral) or splitting attention arm-by-arm.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No retrieved source quantifies neutral vs supinated cable curl 1RM; brachialis-dominant neutral grip is a different enough strength curve that we exclude rather than normalize.

name: Crunch
collapse_rationale: Base bodyweight core exercise; not a qualified variant of another logged lift.

axes.note: Weighted crunch (holding a plate/dumbbell at the chest) is a common progression.

unmapped_notes: Load-mode here adds external resistance rather than changing mechanical advantage on a fixed load, so a strength-coefficient ratio doesn't apply the way it does for grip/stance qualifiers; percentile modeling for weighted vs unweighted crunch (if ever built) should be handled separately, not via this axis.

name: Dip (Chest-Focused)
collapse_rationale: Same bar-dip equipment and pressing pattern as a generic Dip; the defining choice here is a forward torso lean with a wider/flared grip to bias the chest, which is not covered by any axis in the closed vocabulary (grip_width covers hand spacing on a bar/handle in the lateral plane, not torso lean or dip-bar flare angle). Collapsing into Dip but leaving collapse_qualifiers null since it can't be reconstructed from the current axes; the distinguishing detail is captured in unmapped_notes instead.

axes.note: Weighted dips (belt/vest) and assisted-machine dips are both common progressions/regressions.
Wider grip with flared elbows biases pec involvement vs a narrower, elbows-tucked triceps dip.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Coaching sources (FitnessVolt, Steven Fitspot, pullup-dip.com) agree wide/flared grip shifts load toward chest and narrow/tucked toward triceps, but none report a quantified 1RM or max-load ratio between the two grips.

unmapped_notes: The chest-focused vs triceps-focused dip distinction is driven mainly by torso lean angle and elbow flare, neither of which has a dedicated axis in the closed vocabulary (grip_width only captures hand spacing). If this distinction matters enough to track precisely, the vocabulary may need a torso-lean or elbow-flare axis; for now it rides on grip_width as an approximation.

name: EZ-Bar Curl
collapse_rationale: Same standing curl motor pattern as a Barbell Curl; the EZ (cambered) bar is a bar_type qualifier that changes wrist angle and unloaded bar weight, not the exercise itself.

axes.note: EZ bar's angled grips reduce wrist strain and shift emphasis slightly toward brachialis/brachioradialis; straight bar keeps a fully supinated grip and isolates biceps brachii more.
EZ bar has fixed camber points that act as discrete grip-width options.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Multiple coaching sources (SET FOR SET, Inspire US, Strength Warehouse USA) agree straight-bar curls typically allow more total load, attributing it to fuller bicep isolation and a heavier unloaded bar, but none give a quantified working-weight ratio for the same trainee.

name: Glute-Ham Raise
collapse_rationale: Distinct machine/motor pattern (knee-flexion-driven hamstring exercise on a GHD bench); not a qualifier on another logged lift.

axes.note: Progressions run from band-assisted, to bodyweight, to holding a plate/dumbbell.
Beginners often work a partial range near the top before building to a full negative and concentric.

name: High-Bar Squat
collapse_rationale: High-bar vs low-bar is a bar back-rack placement choice, and no axis in the closed 12-axis vocabulary covers bar position on the back (bar_type covers implement, not placement; body_position covers global posture, not this). Rather than force it onto an unrelated axis, High-Bar Squat is kept as its own entry; see unmapped_notes for the load implication.

axes.note: High-bar squats are typically performed with a more upright torso and narrower-to-shoulder stance than low-bar.
Deep/full ATG squats, paused-bottom squats, and box/block squats are common training variants.
Occasionally performed in a Smith machine for a fixed bar path.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No retrieved source quantifies free-bar vs Smith-machine squat load ratio for this exercise specifically.

unmapped_notes: High-bar vs low-bar back placement is a very common real-world qualifier that this vocabulary can't currently express. Research retrieved (PMC8392107, Stronger by Science) indicates low-bar squats generally permit meaningfully more absolute load than high-bar for the same trainee (estimates across sources range roughly 5-20%, e.g. one cited figure of high-bar 1RM being ~80% of low-bar 1RM), so if High-Bar Squat and Low-Bar Squat are ever merged into one base lift with a bar-position axis, that axis's coefficient should almost certainly be 'exclude' or a conservatively low-confidence 'normalize' rather than passthrough — a high-bar-only lifter should not be penalized against a low-bar-heavy percentile population.

name: Inverted Row
collapse_rationale: Distinct bodyweight/horizontal-pull pattern (feet-anchored, body suspended under a bar/rings); not a qualifier on another logged row.

axes.note: Grip changes lat/bicep/rear-delt emphasis similarly to other rows.
Body angle relative to the floor/bar height sets difficulty; more horizontal is harder.
A weighted vest is the common progression once bodyweight reps are easy.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No retrieved source quantifies a pronated vs supinated inverted row load ratio; body-angle also changes effective bodyweight loaded, which the app has no established coefficient for.

unmapped_notes: Body angle (how horizontal the torso is) is the biggest lever on this exercise's effective difficulty, but there's no clean %-bodyweight research retrieved for it; body_position axis is a coarse approximation.

name: Leg Extension
collapse_rationale: Base machine exercise; not itself a qualified variant.

axes.note: Single-leg extension is a common variant for addressing asymmetry.
Lengthened partials (stopping short of full lockout, staying in deep knee flexion) have gained popularity for hypertrophy-focused training.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Per-leg unilateral load is not simply half of bilateral load (no bilateral deficit/facilitation figure retrieved for leg extension specifically); exclude unilateral sets from a bilateral percentile.

name: Meadows Row
collapse_rationale: Landmine-anchored, staggered-stance unilateral row with a distinct bar path/motor pattern; treated as its own base rather than a qualifier on Barbell Row or T-Bar Row.

axes.note: A staggered/split stance is standard for the landmine bar path and torso rotation.
Pronated grip near the sleeve is standard; some use a neutral grip on an attached handle.

unmapped_notes: The landmine sleeve/attachment itself isn't in the `attachment` axis's value list (those values are cable/machine attachments); no change made per the closed-vocabulary rule, but noting the gap.

name: Overhead Triceps Extension
collapse_rationale: Kept as a base name since it spans several distinct implements (dumbbell, EZ-bar, cable) commonly logged under this one label; not collapsing into a more specific variant given the assigned name is already generic.

axes.note: Cable-machine version uses the attachment axis instead of bar_type.

axes.custom_hint: e.g. angled bar
axes.note: Only applies to the cable version.
Seated removes leg drive and forces stricter form.
Single-dumbbell one-arm overhead extension is a common unilateral variant.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No source retrieved comparing one-arm to two-arm overhead extension load; per-arm load is not a clean fraction of the two-arm total.

name: Pogo Hops
collapse_rationale: Bodyweight plyometric drill (rapid ankle-driven hops) with no meaningful equipment or positional variation to qualify; base entry with no axes, per the brief's guidance for plyo/cardio-style entries.

name: Reverse Lunge
collapse_rationale: Direction of the stepping leg (reverse vs forward vs walking lunge) is a distinct motor pattern with different balance/loading demands, and no axis in the closed vocabulary encodes step direction (stance covers static foot width/shape, not a stepping direction); kept as its own base rather than a qualifier on 'Lunge'.

axes.note: Load can be held (DB/KB), back-racked (barbell), or fixed-path (Smith/machine).
Alternating legs each rep, or all reps on one leg before switching.
Common progression from bodyweight to held/loaded to vest.

unmapped_notes: Step direction (reverse vs forward vs walking) is a common qualifier in the wild that this vocabulary can't express as an axis on a single 'Lunge' base; each direction is kept as a separate exercise name for now.

name: Seated Box Jump
collapse_rationale: Distinct plyometric/power drill starting from a dead-stop seated position (removes countermovement); box height is a training-load parameter but isn't covered by any of the 12 axes (rom covers deliberate range restriction on a lift, not jump-target height). No meaningful axis applies.
unmapped_notes: Box height materially changes difficulty but has no home in the closed axis vocabulary; if the app wants to track this, it would need a new axis (out of scope here).

name: Sissy Squat
collapse_rationale: Distinct knee-dominant quad isolation pattern (heels-raised, torso leaning back) with no bar/barbell involvement typically; kept as its own base.

axes.note: Assisted (holding a support, TRX, or machine) is common for beginners; a weighted vest or held plate for advanced lifters.
Full range takes the knees deep into flexion; partials are common early progressions.

name: Stiff-Leg Deadlift
collapse_rationale: Coaching sources (cathe.com, Capital Strength, Barbend) consistently describe the stiff-leg deadlift as a deliberately different movement from the conventional deadlift: hips stay high and shins near-vertical with minimal knee flexion throughout (near-pure hip-hinge, hamstring/glute isolation), versus the conventional deadlift's quad-driven pull off the floor with the shins traveling to the bar. It is not merely a Deadlift + qualifier; kept as its own base. (It is very close to a Romanian Deadlift, but sources note stiff-leg is typically performed from the floor each rep rather than a top-down eccentric-emphasis lift, so it is not collapsed into RDL either.)

axes.note: Dumbbells are common for lighter/higher-rep hamstring work; trap bar changes the hand path slightly.
Stance width has a smaller effect here than in squats since the knees stay mostly locked.
Deficit (standing on a plate) increases the hamstring stretch range; blocks/pauses are used to manage load or reinforce position.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No retrieved source quantifies a deficit-vs-standard stiff-leg deadlift load ratio; deficit work is typically done at reduced load by feel, not a documented fixed percentage.

unmapped_notes: Because stiff-leg deadlift, Romanian deadlift, and conventional deadlift are frequently confused/used interchangeably by lifters (per Capital Strength and Barbend explainer articles), aliases intentionally do not include 'Romanian Deadlift' or 'RDL' to avoid silently merging two exercises with different intended ranges of motion; that merge decision should be a deliberate founder call, not an automatic alias.

name: Trap-Bar Jump
collapse_rationale: Plyometric/power variant performed inside a trap bar (jump squat pattern); the trap bar is the defining implement rather than a swappable qualifier, so it is not collapsed into a generic 'Jump Squat'.

axes.note: Light-to-moderate added load on the trap bar is standard for velocity-based jump training; can also be done with just the bar or bodyweight-only holding the handles.

name: Wrist Curl
collapse_rationale: Kept as its own base rather than collapsing a 'Reverse Wrist Curl' into it: wrist curl (palms up) trains the forearm flexors and reverse wrist curl (palms down) trains the extensors, which are different enough muscle groups/strength curves that treating grip orientation as a simple qualifier risks mixing two different strength capacities under one PR/percentile.

axes.note: Supinated/palms-up trains forearm flexors (standard wrist curl); pronated/palms-down trains forearm extensors (reverse wrist curl) and is markedly weaker.
Dumbbells allow independent per-hand work; EZ bar reduces wrist strain at the bottom of the curl.
Seated with forearms braced on the thighs/bench is standard; kneeling over a bench is an occasional alternative.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Forums and coaching articles (ASFA, GripBoard) agree forearm extensors (pronated/reverse wrist curl) are noticeably weaker than flexors (supinated/standard wrist curl), but no retrieved source gives a quantified load ratio for the same trainee, and the two arguably work different-enough muscle groups that a guessed normalize ratio would be unsafe.

name: Arnold Press
collapse_rationale: The internal rotation-to-external-rotation path through the press is a distinct motor pattern from a straight overhead press, not simply a qualifier of Dumbbell Shoulder Press, so it is tracked as its own lift.

axes.note: Seated is the standard/original version; standing adds a core-stability demand that can reduce usable load.
Alternating Arnold press trades bilateral stability for continuous single-arm pressing.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No dedicated seated-vs-standing Arnold press load comparison was found; magnitude of any reduction is undefined, so exclude rather than guess.

unmapped_notes: Rotation tempo/pause at the bottom is sometimes coached as a distinct cue but is not a load-relevant qualifier and has no axis home.

name: Bench Dip
collapse_rationale: Base bodyweight exercise; not a qualifier of another lift in this list.

axes.custom_hint: e.g. plate held on lap, resistance band assist
axes.note: Assisted (band/partner) reduces effective bodyweight load; added plate/vest increases it.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Assistance amount is user/band-configured rather than a fixed ratio, so no defensible normalization exists.

unmapped_notes: Elevating the feet on a second bench (vs flat on the floor) substantially increases ROM and difficulty but is not captured by any of the 12 axes; flagged for the founder.

name: Cable Crunch
collapse_rationale: Base cable core exercise.

axes.custom_hint: e.g. ab strap, triceps rope with extra loops
axes.note: Rope is the common default for hand/wrist comfort while flexing the spine.
Origin point determines torso flexion angle.
Kneeling is standard; standing versions exist but are less common.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Attachment changes hand/wrist comfort, not the resistance the abs must overcome at a given pin weight.

name: Cable Woodchopper
collapse_rationale: Rotational chop pattern is distinct from any row/press in this list; not a qualifier of another lift here.

axes.note: High origin = high-to-low chop; low origin = low-to-high (rotational uppercut) chop.
Staggered/split stance is common for a more sport-specific rotational base.
Typically trained one side at a time and switched between sets.

axes.custom_hint: e.g. angled chop handle

strength_coefficients.rationale: High-to-low and low-to-high chops load the rotational chain differently enough that comparing pin weights across them is not defensible without dedicated testing.

name: Cuban Press
collapse_rationale: Fetched source (BarBend) explicitly describes the Cuban press as its own three-phase movement (upright row, then external rotation, then overhead press) rather than a variant of another lift.
unmapped_notes: Fetched source (BarBend, https://barbend.com/cuban-press/) frames this as a deliberately light-load, technique/rotator-cuff-prehab movement (typically 5-10 lb dumbbells), not a heavy compound lift, and describes no commonly-practiced load qualifier beyond arm/reach length; axes correctly empty.

name: Donkey Calf Raise
collapse_rationale: Same ankle plantarflexion pattern as a standing calf raise; researched comparisons (Fitness Volt, Gym Plus) frame the donkey version as a body-position variant (hips flexed forward for a deeper stretch and to remove glute-assisted balancing), not a different lift.

axes.note: Bent-over position increases gastrocnemius stretch/ROM and removes glute involvement seen in the standing version.
Historically loaded by a training partner sitting on the hips, a belt-and-plate setup, or a dedicated donkey calf machine (rare in commercial gyms).

axes.note: Machine lateral raise fixes the resistance path; cable lateral raise variants are tracked separately using the attachment/pulley_height axes.
One-arm-at-a-time is common when using a bench for support.
Seated removes the ability to lean/cheat the weight up.

name: Machine Shoulder Press
collapse_rationale: Fixed-path machine pressing is biomechanically different enough from free-weight pressing (no stabilization demand, fixed handle path) that it is tracked as its own base rather than a bar_type qualifier of Overhead Press.

axes.note: Some machines offer both a neutral and a pronated handle position.

unmapped_notes: Machines vary in seat height/back-pad angle by brand, which affects leverage; no axis covers brand-specific machine geometry.

name: Overhead Press
collapse_rationale: Standing barbell press is the classic reference lift for pressing percentiles; kept as its own base (not collapsed into Dumbbell/Machine Shoulder Press, which are separate implements/entries in this library).

axes.note: Seated barbell OHP removes leg drive/lower-body stabilization; standing is the conventional/competition version.
Just-outside-shoulder-width is the most common recommendation; very wide grips shorten ROM but increase shoulder-impingement risk for many lifters.
Smith-machine press removes the need to balance the bar path.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Sources directly disagreed on direction and magnitude (some say seated allows ~7% more due to added stability, others say standing allows more via leg drive); no defensible ratio.
Coaching sources note wide grip shortens ROM (theoretically allowing more load) but changes joint mechanics unfavorably for many lifters; no quantified load ratio was found.

name: Plank
collapse_rationale: Isometric core hold; side plank and other variants are commonly logged as separately named exercises rather than a qualifier of the standard front plank, so this stays as its own base for the prone plank.

axes.note: A weighted vest or plate on the back is sometimes added to progress an otherwise bodyweight hold.

unmapped_notes: Plank is typically tracked by duration, not load, so strength percentile modeling likely doesn't apply to this exercise at all regardless of load_mode.

name: Reverse Curl
collapse_rationale: Same elbow-flexion pattern as a standard curl; the overhand/pronated grip is exactly what the grip_orientation axis exists to describe, and is the classic example of a qualifier-driven variant.

axes.note: Pronated grip shifts emphasis to brachioradialis/forearm extensors and away from the biceps.
EZ-bar reverse curl is common to ease wrist strain from the fully pronated straight-bar grip.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Multiple non-peer-reviewed training sites consistently state lifters must drop load roughly 30-40% for reverse (pronated) curls versus standard (supinated) curls; consistent direction and rough magnitude across sources, but no controlled study, and the movement is arguably a different lift (forearm/brachioradialis-dominant) rather than a true strength-percentile equivalent of the biceps curl.

name: Seal Row
collapse_rationale: Prone, chest-supported row performed on an elevated bench with feet off the floor eliminates any leg drive/momentum, making it a distinctly stricter movement from other supported/bent-over rows; kept as its own base rather than collapsing into a generic Row.

axes.note: Wider grip biases rear delts/upper back; closer grip biases lats and biceps.
Depends on bar/handle used.
Requires a raised bench/platform to hang the bar below.

unmapped_notes: Bench height relative to the bar affects range of motion and difficulty; no axis covers bench/platform height for this movement.

name: Single-Leg Hip Thrust
collapse_rationale: Identical hip-extension pattern to the bilateral hip thrust performed one leg at a time; laterality is exactly the qualifier this describes.

axes.note: Single-leg versions are often performed bodyweight-only or with much lighter external load than bilateral.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Multiple training/coaching sources consistently estimate single-leg hip thrust load capacity at roughly 50-60% of bilateral hip thrust per leg, but this is coaching consensus, not a controlled study with a hard number (an EMG comparison paper on bilateral vs. unilateral barbell hip thrust exists but could not be retrieved to confirm a load ratio). Given the founder's requirement to never penalize a variant-only trainee, excluding these sets from percentile is the safe choice regardless of the exact ratio.

name: Standing Calf Raise
collapse_rationale: Base standing calf-raise entry; machine/barbell/Smith variants differ only by implement and would collapse into this via bar_type if listed separately.

axes.note: Dedicated standing calf-raise machines are most common; Smith-machine and dumbbell-in-hand versions are also practiced.
Many lifters intentionally use a short, partial top-range 'pulse' for peak contraction, distinct from a full stretch-to-contraction rep.
Single-leg calf raise is a common way to increase per-leg load without adding plates.

strength_coefficients.rationale: No comparative load research located; single-leg calf raise load and two-leg calf raise load are not a simple fixed ratio across individuals.

name: Trap Bar Deadlift
collapse_rationale: The trap/hex bar changes hand position (neutral, alongside the body) and torso angle enough that it is generally treated as a biomechanically distinct hinge/squat-hybrid lift from the conventional straight-bar deadlift, not merely a bar_type qualifier of Deadlift; research on the load difference is itself conflicting, reinforcing that it isn't a clean 1:1 substitute.

axes.note: Foot placement inside the frame changes torso angle slightly.
Elevated/block pulls (partial deadlift from blocks or a rack) are sometimes done with a trap bar.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Swinton et al. (2011) found roughly 8% higher 1RM with the trap bar versus a conventional straight-bar deadlift, but Camara et al. (2016) found no significant 1RM difference between the two — the literature is directly conflicting on both magnitude and whether a real difference exists at all, so this is not a safe normalize ratio despite being the most-cited figure.

unmapped_notes: Trap bars vary between low-handle and high-handle designs, which changes the effective ROM and load; no axis distinguishes handle height on the implement itself.

name: Wide-Grip Lat Pulldown
collapse_rationale: Same machine and pulling motor pattern as the standard lat pulldown; grip spacing on the same wide bar is the only difference.

axes.note: Wider grip biases lat width/upper-back stretch; closer grip allows more elbow flexion and biceps contribution.

axes.custom_hint: e.g. angled lat bar, revolving wide bar
axes.note: A dedicated wide lat bar is the standard attachment for this variant.

strength_coefficients.rationale: Multiple coaching/training sites consistently agree wider grip reduces achievable load (estimates range roughly 2-10% less, most commonly cited near 5%), but no peer-reviewed 1RM comparison study was found and the exact figure is unsettled across sources; per the founder's rule, excluding protects a wide-grip-only trainee from being scored against the (heavier) medium-grip reference rather than risking an inaccurate normalize correction.

name: 10K Run
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant of anything else.
unmapped_notes: Meaningful variability (pace/pace zone, surface — road vs trail vs track, elevation gain, negative-split pacing) has no home in the 12-axis vocabulary, which is built for resistance-training equipment/position choices, not endurance-modality parameters.

name: 5K Run
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant of anything else.
unmapped_notes: Same gap as 10K Run: pace zone, surface, and elevation are the real variables here and none map to the closed vocabulary.

name: 90-90 Hip Stretch
collapse_rationale: Base mobility drill, not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Performed with one leg in internal rotation and one in external rotation by definition of the drill (then switched) — this is not a discrete unilateral/bilateral choice the way a carry or curl is, so 'laterality' doesn't cleanly apply. No axis fits.

name: Assault Bike
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant of anything else.
unmapped_notes: Resistance is self-generated fan/air resistance (scales with effort, no damper/level setting) so that gap doesn't apply here unlike rower/ski erg. Some models do support an arms-only or legs-only mode, but that's an upper-vs-lower-body split rather than same-side-limb laterality, and none of the 12 axes represent it — flagging as a real but unmapped variant.

name: Battle Ropes
collapse_rationale: Base cardio/conditioning exercise; not a qualifier variant.

axes.note: Alternating waves (one arm up, one down) vs double/bilateral waves (both arms together) are the two standard, widely-taught patterns and meaningfully change the muscle emphasis: double waves recruit more quad/core stabilization for explosive power, alternating waves emphasize coordination and glute engagement.

unmapped_notes: Rope thickness/length and interval structure (work:rest) also vary in practice but aren't 1RM-style load qualifiers, so no strength coefficient applies.

name: Calf Stretch
collapse_rationale: Base mobility drill; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Commonly done single-leg (staggered-stance wall stretch) or both-legs-at-once (double-leg step-edge stretch), and bent-knee (soleus bias) vs straight-knee (gastrocnemius bias) — real variability, but neither 'stance' nor 'laterality' as defined cleanly captures a static stretch position choice.

name: Cat-Cow
collapse_rationale: Base mobility drill performed in a single fixed quadruped position; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: No commonly-practiced equipment/position choice exists — the drill is defined by its quadruped position and spinal flexion/extension cycle.

name: Couch Stretch
collapse_rationale: Base mobility drill; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Performed one side at a time by design (it's a rear-leg hip flexor stretch) — not a discrete unilateral/bilateral choice in the trainable sense the laterality axis is meant for.

name: Cycling (Outdoor)
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant of anything else.
unmapped_notes: Terrain/elevation gain, gearing/cadence, and seated-vs-standing climbing efforts are the real variables and have no representation in this vocabulary, which targets gym-equipment position/attachment choices rather than outdoor endurance parameters.

name: Elliptical
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant of anything else.
unmapped_notes: Resistance level, incline/ramp setting, and forward-vs-reverse pedaling (reverse biases hamstrings/glutes) are genuine, commonly-used variations on this machine that the closed vocabulary cannot express.

name: Foam Roll Back
collapse_rationale: Base self-myofascial-release drill; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Roller density/texture (smooth vs ridged/rumble) and upper-back-only vs full-spine coverage vary in practice but have no matching axis; also, thoracic rolling is normally bilateral (both sides of the back on the roller at once) so laterality isn't a real choice here the way it is for a single limb.

name: Foam Roll Quads
collapse_rationale: Base self-myofascial-release drill; not a qualifier variant.

axes.note: Rolling both quads at once (bilateral, less pressure per leg) vs one leg at a time with the other foot on the floor for added pressure (unilateral) is a standard, widely-taught choice that changes intensity.

unmapped_notes: Roller firmness/texture also varies but isn't covered by any axis.

name: Hamstring Stretch
collapse_rationale: Base mobility drill; not a qualifier variant.

axes.note: One leg extended at a time (e.g. seated single-leg reach, standing hamstring stretch) vs both legs together (seated or standing forward fold) is a real, commonly-taught choice.

unmapped_notes: Body position also varies widely in practice (seated, standing, lying with a strap) beyond what one axis can cleanly enumerate for a static stretch; kept to the clearest, most consequential choice.

name: Hike
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant of anything else.
unmapped_notes: Elevation gain/terrain and rucking (weighted backpack) are meaningful, commonly-practiced variables. Rucking is close to the 'load_mode' axis's intent, but a loaded hiking backpack isn't the same equipment as a 'weighted_vest' and forcing that value would misrepresent the exercise — flagging rather than misusing the axis.

name: Incline Walk
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality (treadmill or hill incline walking); not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Incline percentage and speed are the exercise's whole point and have no axis in this vocabulary — this is the clearest case in the slice for why a cardio-intensity axis (incline %, resistance level) might be worth adding.

name: Jump Rope
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant.

axes.note: Two-foot bilateral bounce vs alternating-foot 'boxer step' are the two standard footwork patterns taught to beginners and intermediate jumpers.

unmapped_notes: Rope weight and single-unders vs double-unders (two rope passes per jump) are real, commonly-tracked variables with no matching axis.

name: Pigeon Pose
collapse_rationale: Base mobility/yoga drill; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Inherently unilateral (one leg forward, one back) by definition of the pose, not a trainable unilateral/bilateral choice — no axis applies.

name: Rowing (Erg)
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Damper setting / drag factor (typically 3-5 for aerobic work, 120-140 drag factor for speed work per Concept2's own guidance) and stroke rate are the primary trained variables on an erg and have no representation in the 12-axis vocabulary — this is a strong candidate for a dedicated cardio-intensity axis alongside incline % and resistance level.

name: Running (Outdoor)
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant of anything else.
unmapped_notes: Pace zone, terrain (road/trail/track), and elevation gain are the real variables; none map to this vocabulary.

name: Shoulder Dislocates
collapse_rationale: Base mobility drill; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Commonly performed with a rigid dowel/PVC pipe/broomstick or with a resistance band (bands are more forgiving for tight shoulders and add resistance instead of a fixed grip width). This is a genuine equipment choice, but neither 'bar_type' (built for barbell variants) nor 'attachment' (built for cable machines) cleanly covers a dowel or band used this way — flagging rather than forcing it into either axis.

name: Ski Erg
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant.

axes.note: Double-pole technique (both handles pulled together, bilateral) vs alternating single-arm poling is a standard, commonly-taught technique choice on this machine, analogous to battle-rope wave patterns.

unmapped_notes: Resistance/damper setting is the primary intensity variable (same category of gap as Rowing (Erg)) and has no matching axis.

name: Sprint Intervals
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality/protocol; not a qualifier variant of a specific lift.
unmapped_notes: Modality (track, treadmill, bike, hill), work:rest ratio, and incline are the real variables; none map to this vocabulary.

name: Stair Climber
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Step rate and resistance level are the real trained variables and have no matching axis.

name: Stationary Bike
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant.

axes.note: Seated pedaling vs standing/out-of-saddle climbing efforts is a standard, widely-taught choice in spin-style stationary cycling that changes muscular demand.

unmapped_notes: Resistance level (knob or watt target) is the primary intensity variable and has no matching axis — same gap category as Rowing (Erg) and Ski Erg.

name: Swimming (Freestyle)
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Stroke rate, distance-per-stroke, pool vs open-water, and pull-buoy/paddle use are real variables with no matching axis in a vocabulary built around gym equipment/position choices.

name: Thoracic Spine Rotation
collapse_rationale: Base mobility drill; not a qualifier variant.

axes.note: Quadruped/kneeling 'thread the needle' and tall-seated (e.g. on a bench, rotating with arms crossed) are both commonly taught setups. Side-lying 'open book' is also widely used but has no matching value in the body_position vocabulary (lying_supine/lying_prone don't represent side-lying), so it's omitted rather than misrepresented.

unmapped_notes: The side-lying open-book variant is a real, very commonly taught setup that the body_position vocabulary cannot represent (no side-lying value) — flagging this gap explicitly rather than approximating it with lying_supine or lying_prone.

name: Treadmill Run
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Incline % and speed are the exercise's core trained variables and have no axis in this vocabulary.

name: Treadmill Walk
collapse_rationale: Base cardio modality; not a qualifier variant.
unmapped_notes: Incline % and speed are the core trained variables. Backward/retro walking on a treadmill is also a real, commonly-used variant (posterior chain/knee-rehab emphasis) with no direction axis in this vocabulary — flagging alongside the incline % gap.
